abstract: Species introductions and transplants offer powerful contexts to understand evolutionary patterns and processes, and they are increasingly critical for conservation. However, introduction success varies widely, and predicting outcomes remains challenging. Using multiple source populations should increase the chance of introduction success, while also providing an opportunity to explore the factors that predict success of individual source populations in the same environment. We used replicated, mixed-population introductions of >12,000 threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) to test whether source population success could be predicted by environmental matching between source and recipient environments and/or by source population characteristics. We introduced four to eight source populations of stickleback into each of nine natural lakes with no other stickleback and tracked their relative success over the following 2 years (up to two generations). Source population success was largely consistent across lakes, despite divergent environmental conditions. These results point to the importance of consistent source population differences rather than environmental matching in determining introduction success in natural settings. Source populations that were consistently successful tended to have greater stress tolerance and higher genetic diversity, though these relationships were not conclusive. Our study highlights the value of considering factors that generate fitness differences independent of environmental context when predicting ecological and evolutionary dynamics and planning conservation programs.
